about: Building materials (roadmap BT3a): Brick and tile (wall materials, bonds and brick techniques; roof tiles are in another file). Fields as bidb/building_materials.py.

materials.name: Roman brick and tile

period.text: made in Britain during the Roman occupation, AD 43 to 410 (the Romans brought fired brick with them; a Scottish source says brick came in with them in the first century AD); after it came a gap of 600-700 years in brick-making, while Roman brick was taken from ruins and reused in Anglo-Saxon and Norman buildings (St Albans, Brixworth, Colchester)

regions.text: Roman Britain (England and Wales, briefly southern Scotland); reused near Roman towns such as Verulamium (St Albans) and Colchester

materials.technology: Legionary mobile kilns; thin bricks laid as levelling courses (bonding tiles) in flint and rubble walls. When Roman rule ended the craft lapsed, and later builders robbed Roman sites for brick.

examples.name: All Saints' Church, Brixworth
examples.note: Anglo-Saxon church (founded about 680) built with reused Roman brick

examples.name: St Albans Cathedral
examples.note: Norman abbey church (building began in 1077, when Abbot Paul of Caen arrived) with a crossing tower on massive piers of Roman brick from Verulamium

examples.name: Colchester Castle
examples.note: Norman keep (begun 1076 according to the late 13th-century Colchester Chronicle) of coursed rubble with Roman brick and tile robbed from nearby ruins

materials.note: Archaeologists often call Roman brick and tile together ceramic building material (CBM), since fragments of wall brick and roof or floor tile are hard to tell apart.

materials.name: Brick

period.text: brick-making revived in eastern England after the Roman gap: the earliest dated surviving post-Roman brickwork a source here names is the lancet windows of the chapel of St Nicholas at Coggeshall Abbey, Essex, dated to the 1220s (one source puts the revival in 12th-century East Anglia, another in the late 13th and early 14th centuries); its use rose sharply after the Restoration of 1660 and peaked in the Victorian period (1830-1914), when more bricks were made than in all earlier periods; still made

regions.text: first eastern England (East Anglia, Essex, Hull and Beverley) where good stone was lacking; Tudor brick across south-east England; in Scotland a brief Roman use, a little in the 17th century and in earnest from the 18th; in Ireland from the 1630s (Jigginstown, Co. Kildare); everywhere with the railways

materials.technology: Revived through trade with the Low Countries, which already had a large brick industry; Tudor bricks were made on site in clamps fired with wood, heather or turf; after the Great Fire of London (1666) timber framing was no longer acceptable in towns; the brick tax (1784-1850) raised its price; mechanised making from the mid-19th century and the railways spread uniform bricks everywhere

materials.note: Sources differ on when brick-making restarted: Little Wenham Hall's article says the 12th century in East Anglia; Gerard Lynch says the late 13th and early 14th centuries in eastern England. The Coggeshall chapel's brick (1220s) is the earliest dated example here.

sources.title: Brick tax

sources.quote: The brick tax was a property tax introduced in Great Britain in 1784, during the reign of King George III, to help pay for the wars in the American Colonies.

materials.name: Diaper brickwork (Tudor)

period.text: the earliest dated example a source here names is Fulham Palace (late 15th century, the Tudor courtyard probably begun by Bishop Kempe about 1480); characteristic of 16th-century Tudor brickwork; the Tudor fashion ended with the Tudor period (1603), and diaper patterns came back with Victorian polychrome brickwork (see that entry)

regions.text: Tudor brick buildings of south-east and eastern England (London, Essex, Norfolk, Surrey...)

materials.technology: Headers over-burnt or vitrified in wood-fired clamps came out dark (purple to slate, stained by the potash of the fuel); laid in English bond, they made lozenges and chequers in the red brick

examples.name: Fulham Palace

materials.name: English bond

period.text: the oldest regular bond: the earliest work a source here ties to it is Tudor brickwork (the late 15th and 16th centuries; the date given is the start of Tudor diaper work at Fulham, about 1480; Little Wenham Hall, c. 1270, was built before the standard bonds); commonly used until Flemish bond overtook it (by the mid-17th century for the best work, generally by the end of the 17th or the start of the 18th); still preferred for engineering and industrial work

regions.text: England and wherever brick was laid in the isles

materials.technology: Alternate courses of stretchers and headers, with no continuous vertical joints in the wall's thickness: the strongest bond, so engineers kept it for industrial buildings and civil engineering

sources.title: A guide to brick bonding patterns
sources.author: Wienerberger UK (brick maker)
sources.quote: The traditional English brick bond alternates between stretcher and header courses, with headers centred over the stretchers underneath.

sources.title: A guide to brick bonding patterns

materials.name: Flemish bond

period.text: the Dutch House at Kew (Kew Palace), 1631, is thought to be the first example in England (the earliest known whole facade in correct Flemish bond); preferred for high-quality brickwork by the mid-17th century and the usual face bond of Georgian building; the main domestic bond of the Victorians; still used

regions.text: England first (London), then throughout the isles and the colonies

materials.technology: Headers and stretchers alternate in each course; dark burnt or glazed headers could pattern it; the bond came with Dutch fashions, though it did not begin in Flanders

examples.name: Kew Palace (the Dutch House)
examples.note: thought to be the first example of Flemish bond in England

materials.note: Despite its name the bond did not begin in Flanders; it was used across northern and central Europe in the late Middle Ages. Sources differ on when it overtook English bond: by the middle of the 17th century (Wikipedia) or from the beginning of the 18th century (Wienerberger).

sources.title: Flemish bond
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The pattern features bricks laid lengthwise (stretchers) alternating with bricks laid with their shorter ends exposed (headers) within the same courses.

materials.name: Stretcher bond

period.text: the bond of the half-brick outer leaf of the cavity wall, so it became the usual face of brick buildings when most new outside walls in the UK became cavity walls, from the 1920s (the date given; half-brick walls are older, but no source here dates them); still the commonest bond

materials.technology: Only possible in a wall half a brick thick, tied by metal wall ties to an inner leaf across the cavity; English or Flemish bond can be imitated on the outer leaf with half bricks (snap headers)

sources.title: A guide to brick bonding patterns
sources.author: Wienerberger UK (brick maker)
sources.quote: As the outer leaf of a building envelope is now only half a brick thick in modern construction, stretcher bond has become the most popular bond as it is time and cost effective to use.

sources.quote: Chinese bonds were in use in the late 19th century but by the 1920s had largely been displaced by the cavity wall (ie Stretcher Bond).

sources.title: A guide to brick bonding patterns
sources.author: Wienerberger UK (brick maker)
sources.quote: With the stretcher bond, courses are laid as stretchers with the joint of one course falling midway between the joints of the courses below.

sources.quote: Flemish bonds can be replicated in the half-brick outer leaf of a cavity wall by using whole bricks as stretchers, while the headers are created by half bricks called bats or snap-headers.

sources.title: Brick bonds
sources.author: J. A. Harrison (jaharrison.me.uk)
sources.quote: When cavity walls were introduced in the early 20th century, this was often offset by using half bricks to emulate the appearance of Flemish Bond.

materials.name: Cavity wall

period.text: rare examples in the 18th and 19th centuries (the date given, 1700, is the start of the 18th century; Wikipedia instead says cavity walls were reintroduced in the UK in the 19th century); the usual outside wall of new UK buildings since the 1920s; insulation in the cavity standard from the 1970s and required by building codes from the 1990s

materials.technology: Early cavity walls were tied with headers spanning the cavity; metal wall ties from the second half of the 19th century, common by about 1900; cavity insulation from the 1970s
materials.note: Sources differ on the start: Designing Buildings puts rare early examples in the 18th and 19th centuries, Wikipedia says they were reintroduced (after Greek and Roman use) in the 19th century.

sources.title: Cavity wall

sources.quote: A cavity wall is a type of wall that has an airspace between the outer face and the inner, usually structural, construction.

sources.title: Cavity wall

sources.title: Cavity wall

sources.title: Cavity wall

sources.title: Cavity wall
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.quote: The introduction of insulation into the cavity became standard in the 1970s and then required by most building codes in the 1990s.

materials.name: Gauged (rubbed) brickwork

period.text: an early form, introduced from the Netherlands, on the Dutch House at Kew (1631); popularised by Wren in the late 17th century; after 1730 too expensive for whole facades and kept for arches, aprons and ornament; used for Victorian enrichment and still carved by conservation craftsmen

regions.text: London and the south-east first, then fine brick buildings everywhere

materials.technology: Soft, fine 'rubbing bricks' cut with the brick axe and rubbed to exact sizes after firing, laid with very thin joints of lime putty

materials.name: Mathematical tile

period.text: 18th and early 19th centuries: black glazed tiles in Brighton from about 1760 (Patcham Place was clad in them when rebuilt in 1764); the latest dated example a source here names is the Jireh Chapel, Lewes, built in 1805

regions.text: south-east England, above all East Sussex (Brighton, Lewes) and Kent; also Wiltshire, Surrey and Hampshire

materials.technology: Tiles hung on laths over timber-framed walls and pointed in lime mortar to look like brickwork (header or stretcher bond); cheaper and easier to lay than brick and resistant to sea spray. Whether the brick tax (1784-1850) encouraged them is disputed: the tiles were taxed too.

materials.name: Machine-made and pressed brick

period.text: the first British brick-making machine patent a source here names is Bradley & Craven's stiff-plastic machine of 1853 (Henry Clayton's machine of 1855 made up to 25,000 bricks a day); mechanisation spread from the mid-19th century and after 1850 manufactured bricks replaced handmade ones; extruded and pressed facing bricks in Scotland in the mid-to-late 19th century; still how most bricks are made

regions.text: throughout the isles; in Scotland extruded and pressed facing bricks from the late 19th century

materials.technology: Patented brick-making machines (stiff-plastic pressing, extrusion and wire cutting) and continuous kilns: Friedrich Hoffmann patented his kiln in 1858, and by 1867 fifty were working in England; railways carried the bricks everywhere.
